props.title: Planet Hulk
props.initialSlug: Animated adaptation of popular comic storyline

sections.content: Planet Hulk (2010) adapts one of Marvel's most ambitious Hulk storylines, transforming Banner's rage monster into a gladiatorial champion on an alien world. This animated feature pulls from the groundbreaking 2006-2007 comic run, delivering brutal arena combat that even Thor: Ragnarok (2017) would later reference. The film strips away Banner entirely, focusing on Hulk's evolution from slave to revolutionary leader - a sharp departure from Earth-bound stories like The Incredible Hulk (1977) or Ang Lee's Hulk (2003).

sections.content: The animation style builds on Marvel's previous direct-to-video successes like Ultimate Avengers (2006) and Doctor Strange: The Sorcerer Supreme (2007), but with significantly more violence and mature themes. The alien world of Sakaar comes alive through detailed world-building and distinctive character designs that feel more Heavy Metal (1981) than typical superhero fare. The film's willingness to embrace darker themes sets it apart from contemporary animated superhero films like Batman: Under the Red Hood (2010).

What makes Planet Hulk particularly compelling is its exploration of leadership and belonging. Unlike The Avengers (2012) where Hulk functions as a team player, or The Incredible Hulk (2008) where he's hunted on Earth, this story gives Hulk agency and purpose beyond destruction. The gladiatorial elements echo classics like Spartacus (1960), while the sci-fi setting draws from space epics like John Carter (2012). SUBHEAD: Animation and Violence in Superhero Storytelling

sections.content: Planet Hulk represents a pivotal moment in Marvel's animated features, pushing violence boundaries similarly to DC's Justice League Dark (2017) and Batman: The Dark Knight Returns (2012). The film's success helped pave the way for more mature animated superhero stories like Batman: The Long Halloween (2021) and Invincible (2021). The fighting sequences are brutal and consequential, more aligned with anime influences like Ninja Scroll (1993) than Western animation traditions.
